roles.name: Software Engineer
roles.blurb: The generalist who designs, builds, tests and ships production software across the stack. Days mix writing code, reviewing PRs, debugging incidents, and translating fuzzy product asks into working systems.

roles.name: Backend Engineer
roles.blurb: Owns the server-side logic, data models, and APIs that power an application. Heavy on databases, throughput, reliability, and getting distributed services to talk to each other without falling over.

roles.name: Frontend Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds the interfaces users actually touch — components, state, performance, and pixel-accurate layouts. Lives in JavaScript/TypeScript and a framework like React, obsessing over load times and accessibility.

roles.name: Full-Stack Engineer
roles.blurb: Owns a feature end-to-end, from the database schema up to the UI. Prized at startups and lean teams for shipping whole slices of product without handoffs; a jack of all layers.

roles.name: Web Developer
roles.blurb: Builds and maintains websites and web apps, often in agencies or in-house marketing/product teams. More CMS, templating, and cross-browser work than deep systems; increasingly squeezed by no-code and AI tooling.

roles.name: API Engineer
roles.blurb: Specializes in designing, versioning, and scaling the APIs other teams and customers build on. Deep on contracts, auth, gateways, and developer experience — the plumbing that makes integrations feel effortless.

roles.name: Software Architect
roles.blurb: Sets the high-level technical direction across systems — patterns, boundaries, tech choices, and non-functional requirements. Less hands-on coding, more design docs, trade-off calls, and aligning many teams on one blueprint.

roles.name: Staff Engineer
roles.blurb: A senior individual contributor who drives ambiguous, cross-team technical work without managing people. Multiplies other engineers through architecture, mentorship, and taste — the technical spine of an org.

roles.name: Principal Engineer
roles.blurb: The most senior IC rung below fellow — owns technical strategy that spans the whole org and sets multi-year direction. Deep, broad, and highly leveraged; part architect, part force-of-nature problem solver.

roles.name: Technical Lead
roles.blurb: A senior engineer who owns the technical execution of a team — breaking down work, unblocking people, and keeping delivery on track. Half coding, half coordination, often the bridge to the product manager.

roles.name: Distributed Systems Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds systems that stay correct and fast across many machines — consensus, replication, partitioning, and failure handling. High-scale, low-level work where a single race condition can take down a fleet.

roles.name: Java Developer
roles.blurb: Backend engineer specialized in the Java/Spring ecosystem, the workhorse of banks, telcos, and large enterprises. Steady, well-paid, and everywhere — mostly microservices, transactions, and legacy modernization.

roles.name: Python Developer
roles.blurb: Builds backends, tooling, and automation in Python — Django/FastAPI web services one day, data plumbing or scripting the next. Riding a demand wave thanks to Python's grip on AI and data work.

roles.name: Node.js Developer
roles.blurb: Backend developer working in the JavaScript/TypeScript runtime — Express or NestJS services, real-time apps, and API layers. Popular at startups where one language spans front and back.

roles.name: Go Engineer
roles.blurb: Writes high-performance backend and infrastructure services in Go, the go-to language for cloud-native tooling and microservices. Concurrency-heavy, systems-flavored work that carries a market premium.

roles.name: .NET Developer
roles.blurb: Builds enterprise applications and services on Microsoft's stack — C#, ASP.NET Core, and Azure. Common in finance, healthcare, and corporate IT; stable demand, steady pay.

roles.name: Ruby on Rails Developer
roles.blurb: Ships product fast in Ruby on Rails, a favorite of startups and SaaS companies for its productivity. A smaller, tighter market than it once was — but the ones hiring still pay well.

roles.name: Application Developer
roles.blurb: A broad enterprise role building and maintaining business applications to spec — internal tools, line-of-business systems, and integrations. Common in corporate IT and consultancies; generalist and framework-driven.

roles.name: Java Backend Engineer
roles.blurb: Build and maintain server-side business logic and APIs for large-scale enterprise systems — banking cores, e-commerce backends, and JVM microservices. Day-to-day is Spring services, JPA/Hibernate data access, and keeping high-throughput systems stable under load.

roles.name: Spring Boot Engineer
roles.blurb: Design microservices and REST/gRPC APIs on the Spring ecosystem — Spring Boot, Spring Cloud, Spring Security — wiring together data stores, message queues, and cloud infra. The workhorse role of enterprise Java shops and fintech backends.

roles.name: Python Backend Engineer
roles.blurb: Write server-side services and APIs in Python — FastAPI, Django, or Flask — powering web apps, data platforms, and ML-serving layers. Work spans API design, async I/O, database modeling, and gluing together the vast Python ecosystem.

roles.name: Django Developer
roles.blurb: Build full-featured web backends on Django — models, the ORM, admin, auth, and DRF APIs — for content platforms, SaaS products, and marketplaces. Batteries-included framework work with a heavy ORM and templating flavor.

roles.name: Rust Engineer
roles.blurb: Write memory-safe, high-performance systems code in Rust — backend services, blockchain and crypto infrastructure, databases, and performance-critical components. The draw is speed with safety; the cost is a steep borrow-checker learning curve.

roles.name: .NET / C# Engineer
roles.blurb: Build backend services and enterprise applications on .NET with C# — ASP.NET Core APIs, Entity Framework data access, and Azure-hosted services. Common in enterprise, government, healthcare, and Windows-centric shops.

roles.name: C++ Engineer
roles.blurb: Write performance-critical native code in modern C++ — game engines, embedded systems, databases, browsers, and desktop applications. Deep in memory management, templates, and squeezing every cycle out of the hardware.

roles.name: Low-Latency C++ Engineer
roles.blurb: Engineer ultra-low-latency trading systems in C++ for HFT and market-making firms — nanoseconds matter, so you profile cache misses, avoid hot-path allocations, and co-design with hardware. Among the highest-paid engineering roles anywhere.

roles.name: Ruby on Rails Engineer
roles.blurb: Build and scale web applications on Ruby on Rails — the convention-over-configuration framework behind Shopify, GitHub, and Basecamp. Fast feature delivery with ActiveRecord, background jobs, and a mature testing culture.

roles.name: PHP Developer
roles.blurb: Maintain and build web backends in PHP — still powering a huge share of the web via WordPress, custom CMS, and e-commerce. Work ranges from legacy maintenance to modern, strongly typed PHP 8.

roles.name: Laravel Developer
roles.blurb: Build modern PHP web applications and APIs on Laravel — Eloquent ORM, Blade templates, queues, and the rich Laravel ecosystem (Forge, Nova, Livewire). Popular for SaaS, admin panels, and agency product work.

roles.name: Node.js Engineer
roles.blurb: Build backend services and APIs on Node.js — event-driven, non-blocking servers powering real-time apps, REST/GraphQL APIs, and BFF layers. Heavy use of Express/Nest, the npm ecosystem, and increasingly TypeScript.

roles.name: TypeScript Backend Engineer
roles.blurb: Build type-safe backend services in TypeScript — NestJS, tRPC, and Node runtimes — where the appeal is end-to-end type safety from database to API. Common at product companies that share types across frontend and backend.

roles.name: Scala Engineer
roles.blurb: Build backend and data-intensive systems in Scala — functional, strongly typed JVM code using Akka, Play, or Cats, and often Spark for large-scale data. Popular in fintech, adtech, and streaming-data platforms.

roles.name: Elixir Engineer
roles.blurb: Build highly concurrent, fault-tolerant backends in Elixir on the BEAM/OTP — Phoenix web apps, real-time systems, and messaging platforms that handle millions of connections. A scarce but beloved niche.

roles.name: Kotlin Backend Engineer
roles.blurb: Build server-side services in Kotlin — modern, concise JVM code with Spring Boot or Ktor — increasingly the default for new JVM backends and a common migration target from Java. Popular in fintech and product engineering.

roles.name: Clojure Engineer
roles.blurb: Build backend systems in Clojure — a functional, dynamically typed Lisp on the JVM prized for its REPL-driven workflow and immutable data. Found in fintech, healthcare, and data-heavy startups that value expressiveness.

roles.name: Perl Developer
roles.blurb: Maintain and extend Perl systems — legacy web backends, sysadmin automation, bioinformatics pipelines, and text-processing tooling. Demand is declining and mostly maintenance-driven, but specialists stay valuable where large Perl codebases live.

roles.name: .NET Full Stack Engineer
roles.blurb: Build end-to-end enterprise web apps on the Microsoft stack — ASP.NET Core on the backend plus Blazor, Angular, or React on the front — with SQL Server and Azure. The versatile generalist role of the .NET world.

roles.name: Mobile Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds and ships consumer or enterprise apps on iOS and/or Android — screens, offline state, API integration, and the App Store/Play release cycle. Day to day is UI work, wrangling platform quirks, and chasing crash-free rates.

roles.name: iOS Engineer
roles.blurb: Specializes in Apple platforms — Swift, SwiftUI/UIKit, and the tight Xcode/Instruments loop. The work is pixel-accurate UI, async data flow, and staying ahead of each WWDC release.

roles.name: Android Engineer
roles.blurb: Owns the Android app — Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, coroutines, and the Gradle build. Balances a huge device/OS matrix, background execution limits, and Play Console releases.

roles.name: React Native Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds one JavaScript/TypeScript codebase that ships to both stores, dropping into native modules when the bridge isn't enough. Common at startups and agencies that want iOS+Android from one team.

roles.name: Flutter Developer
roles.blurb: Ships cross-platform apps in Dart with Flutter's widget system and a single rendering engine. Popular for pixel-consistent UI across iOS, Android, and increasingly web/desktop.

roles.name: Mobile Architect
roles.blurb: Sets the technical direction for a company's mobile estate — modularization, cross-platform strategy, build/release pipelines, and performance budgets across many apps and teams. Mostly design, review, and cross-team influence rather than daily feature code.

roles.name: Cross-Platform Mobile Engineer
roles.blurb: Focuses on maximizing shared code across iOS and Android via React Native, Flutter, or KMP while dropping to native where it matters. The craft is drawing the line between shared logic and platform-specific UX.

roles.name: Kotlin Multiplatform Engineer
roles.blurb: Shares business logic (and increasingly UI via Compose Multiplatform) across Android and iOS from a single Kotlin codebase, interoperating with Swift on the Apple side. A fast-rising niche as KMP goes production-stable.

roles.name: Mobile Game Developer
roles.blurb: Builds games for phones — gameplay loops, physics, and heavy performance and battery optimization within tight memory budgets. Ships in Unity or Unreal and lives with monetization/ads SDKs and live-ops.

roles.name: Unity Developer
roles.blurb: Builds interactive 3D/2D clients in Unity with C# — games, AR experiences, simulations, and increasingly non-gaming real-time apps. Work spans gameplay scripting, the asset pipeline, and squeezing frame rates on target hardware.

roles.name: Unreal Engine Developer
roles.blurb: Builds high-fidelity clients in Unreal with C++ and Blueprints — AAA games, and increasingly automotive, film virtual production, and simulation. Deep engine, rendering, and performance work on the client side.

roles.name: Game Client Engineer
roles.blurb: Owns the client side of a game — gameplay systems, rendering integration, netcode, and tools — whether on a commercial engine or a custom one. Sits between designers and backend/server engineers to make the moment-to-moment feel right.

roles.name: Mobile SDK Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds the SDKs other developers embed — payments, analytics, maps, auth — as polished Swift and Kotlin libraries. The work is API design, ruthless backward compatibility, small binary size, and great docs and sample apps.

roles.name: Mobile Platform Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds the internal foundations that product teams build on — build systems, modularization, developer tooling, and app-size/performance guardrails. An enablement role: your customers are other mobile engineers.

roles.name: Mobile Release / DevOps Engineer
roles.blurb: Automates the path from commit to store — Fastlane pipelines, code signing and provisioning, phased rollouts, and crash/release monitoring. Keeps iOS and Android releases fast, repeatable, and un-broken.

roles.name: Mobile QA Automation Engineer
roles.blurb: Owns quality for mobile apps — test strategy plus automated suites in Appium, Espresso, and XCUITest running across device farms in CI. Balances flaky-test firefighting, real-device coverage, and release sign-off.

roles.name: Mobile AR Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds augmented-reality features on phones and headsets with ARKit/ARCore (and RealityKit/AR Foundation) — plane detection, occlusion, 3D rendering, and spatial UX. A specialized niche riding new device launches.

roles.name: Mobile Product Manager
roles.blurb: Owns the roadmap and outcomes for a mobile app — prioritizing features against store constraints, running A/B tests, and steering ASO and mobile analytics. Lives between engineering, design, and growth, measured on retention and app metrics.

roles.name: Data Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds and maintains the pipelines that move, clean, and reshape data from source systems into warehouses and lakes so analysts and models can trust it. Day-to-day is SQL, Python, orchestration DAGs, and firefighting broken loads at 2am.

roles.name: Analytics Engineer
roles.blurb: Lives in the transformation layer: turns raw warehouse tables into clean, tested, documented models that analysts query. Owns dbt projects, semantic definitions, and the metrics everyone argues about. Half software engineer, half analyst.

roles.name: ETL Developer
roles.blurb: Builds extract-transform-load jobs, often on established stacks (Informatica, SSIS, Talend, DataStage) feeding enterprise warehouses. Steady, spec-driven work heavy on batch schedules and data validation; increasingly migrating legacy flows to cloud ELT.

roles.name: Data Platform Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds the internal platform other data teams stand on: the orchestration, catalog, storage, compute, and self-serve tooling. Thinks in abstractions and paved roads rather than individual pipelines — infra engineer who specializes in data systems.

roles.name: Streaming Data Engineer
roles.blurb: Designs low-latency pipelines that process events as they happen — Kafka, Flink, Spark Streaming, Kinesis. Wrestles with exactly-once semantics, windowing, backpressure, and state. When the pipeline is measured in milliseconds, this is who owns it.

roles.name: Data Warehouse Engineer
roles.blurb: Owns the warehouse itself — schema design, partitioning, clustering, performance tuning, and cost control on Snowflake, Redshift, BigQuery or Synapse. Turns messy source data into star schemas that queries fly through and finance doesn't complain about.

roles.name: BI Engineer / BI Developer
roles.blurb: Bridges the warehouse and the business: builds the semantic models, dashboards, and reporting datasets in Looker, Power BI, or Tableau that executives actually look at. Part data modeling, part visualization craft, part stakeholder wrangling.

roles.name: Big Data Engineer
roles.blurb: Handles data at terabyte-to-petabyte scale on distributed frameworks — Spark, Hadoop, Hive, Presto. Optimizes shuffles, joins, and cluster resources so batch jobs over enormous datasets finish before the SLA. Increasingly a cloud-lakehouse variant of the classic Hadoop role.

roles.name: Data Architect
roles.blurb: Designs the enterprise data landscape — how warehouses, lakes, streaming, governance, and access all fit together across an org. Sets standards, picks platforms, models domains, and reviews everyone else's designs. Senior, strategy-heavy, light on daily coding.

roles.name: DataOps Engineer
roles.blurb: Applies DevOps discipline to data: CI/CD for pipelines, environment management, observability, alerting, and automated testing so data ships reliably. Keeps the pipeline fleet green and reduces the toil of deploying and monitoring data workflows.

roles.name: Data Infrastructure Engineer
roles.blurb: Runs the low-level guts of data systems — the clusters, storage layers, query engines, and message buses that everything else depends on. Deep systems work: reliability, scaling, capacity, and performance of databases and distributed data services.

roles.name: Cloud Data Engineer
roles.blurb: A data engineer specialized in one cloud's native stack — Glue/Redshift/Lambda on AWS, Dataflow/BigQuery on GCP, or Data Factory/Synapse on Azure. Builds serverless, managed pipelines and knows the cost and IAM footguns of the platform cold.

roles.name: Snowflake Data Engineer
roles.blurb: A data engineer built around the Snowflake ecosystem — warehouses, Snowpark, Streams & Tasks, cost governance, and the surrounding dbt/Fivetran tooling. In demand wherever a company has bet its analytics stack on Snowflake.

roles.name: Databricks / Lakehouse Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds on the Databricks lakehouse — Delta Lake, Unity Catalog, Spark on Databricks, and increasingly Databricks SQL and ML workflows. Merges the warehouse and lake worlds; a hot specialization as lakehouse architectures take over.

roles.name: Data Integration Engineer
roles.blurb: Connects systems — APIs, SaaS apps, databases, files — so data flows between them reliably. Works with iPaaS and ELT connectors (Fivetran, Mulesoft, Boomi), handles auth, schema drift, and reconciliation. The plumbing specialist for heterogeneous stacks.

roles.name: Data Quality Engineer
roles.blurb: Owns whether the data is actually right. Builds validation frameworks, anomaly detection, tests, and observability so bad data gets caught before it reaches a dashboard or a model. Great Expectations, dbt tests, and a lot of detective work.

roles.name: Kafka / Streaming Platform Engineer
roles.blurb: Runs the event-streaming backbone as a platform — Kafka/Confluent clusters, schema registry, connect, and the reliability and scaling of it all. Not building one pipeline but operating the nervous system that hundreds of pipelines ride on.

roles.name: Apache Spark Engineer
roles.blurb: A deep specialist in Spark — writing, tuning, and debugging large-scale batch and streaming jobs, understanding the Catalyst optimizer, partitioning, and shuffle behavior. Called in when Spark jobs are slow, expensive, or falling over.

roles.name: Data Modeler
roles.blurb: Designs the logical and physical structure of data — entities, relationships, keys, dimensional and normalized schemas — so warehouses and applications are consistent and query-friendly. Precise, standards-driven work at the intersection of business and database design.

roles.name: Data Pipeline Engineer
roles.blurb: Focuses squarely on building and operating ingestion and transformation pipelines end to end — sources, orchestration, transforms, loads, and monitoring. A hands-on flavor of data engineer whose whole job is the moving-data machinery.

roles.name: Real-Time Analytics Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds systems that serve fresh analytics with sub-second latency — real-time OLAP on ClickHouse, Druid, Pinot, or Materialize feeding live dashboards, personalization, and operational metrics. Where streaming meets analytics query serving.

roles.name: Head of Data Engineering
roles.blurb: Leads the data engineering org — sets platform strategy, hires and grows the team, owns reliability and cost of the whole data estate, and translates business needs into a roadmap. Mostly people, priorities, and architecture calls rather than code.

roles.name: Data Scientist
roles.blurb: Turns messy business questions into data problems: pulls and cleans data, builds models and experiments, and translates results into decisions for product and leadership. A generalist role that swings between SQL wrangling, statistics, and storytelling.

roles.name: Applied Scientist
roles.blurb: Sits between research and engineering at big tech and product companies: designs ML models grounded in current research, then ships them into real systems. PhD-heavy, with a strong publish-and-productionize mandate.

roles.name: Research Scientist
roles.blurb: Pushes the frontier: formulates novel methods, runs experiments, and publishes at venues like NeurIPS or ICML, often at industrial labs or research orgs. Deep theoretical grounding and a long time horizon on impact.

roles.name: Machine Learning Scientist
roles.blurb: Owns the modeling science behind ML products: chooses architectures, designs training and evaluation, and improves model quality metrics. More research-leaning than an ML engineer, more product-leaning than a pure research scientist.

roles.name: Statistician
roles.blurb: Designs studies and applies rigorous statistical methods to draw valid conclusions from data — in government, healthcare, research, and industry. Strong on experimental design, inference, and sampling; often the guardian of methodological correctness.

roles.name: Biostatistician
roles.blurb: Applies statistics to clinical trials, epidemiology, and public health: designs trials, writes statistical analysis plans, and produces the analyses regulators rely on. Heavily used in pharma, biotech, and academic medicine.

roles.name: Econometrician
roles.blurb: Builds economic and causal models from data: estimates demand, elasticity, and treatment effects using econometric methods. Found in tech economics teams, central banks, policy shops, and consulting, bridging economics and data science.

roles.name: Quantitative Analyst
roles.blurb: The 'quant' on the sell-side or in risk/pricing: builds pricing models, risk measures, and analytics for derivatives and portfolios. Heavy on stochastic calculus, numerical methods, and clean, fast code under regulatory scrutiny.

roles.name: Quantitative Researcher
roles.blurb: The buy-side alpha hunter at hedge funds and prop shops: researches signals, builds and backtests trading strategies, and squeezes edge out of noisy market data. Extremely competitive, math-heavy, and bonus-driven.

roles.name: Quantitative Trader
roles.blurb: Runs systematic and semi-systematic strategies in live markets: manages risk, executes, and iterates on models under real P&L. Fast-paced, quantitative, and deeply tied to trading performance and bonuses.

roles.name: Experimentation Scientist
roles.blurb: Owns the science of A/B testing at scale: designs trustworthy experiments, builds the stats behind the testing platform, and stops teams from shipping on noise. Deep on variance reduction, sequential testing, and causal validity.

roles.name: Decision Scientist
roles.blurb: Applies data science to business decisions rather than production models: frames problems, quantifies tradeoffs, and hands leaders defensible recommendations. Heavy on analysis, causal thinking, and communication over ML deployment.

roles.name: Actuary
roles.blurb: Prices risk for insurance and pensions: models mortality, claims, and reserves, and signs off on financial soundness. A credential-driven profession — progress is gated by a long series of actuarial exams — combining statistics, finance, and regulation.

roles.name: NLP Research Scientist
roles.blurb: Specializes in language: builds and adapts models for understanding and generating text, from LLM fine-tuning to retrieval and evaluation. Rides at the center of the generative-AI wave, blending research with applied model work.

roles.name: Computer Vision Scientist
roles.blurb: Builds models that see: detection, segmentation, tracking, and generation over images and video, for autonomy, medical imaging, robotics, and AR. Combines deep learning research with hard real-world data and latency constraints.

roles.name: Product Data Scientist
roles.blurb: The analytics brain embedded in a product team: defines metrics, sizes opportunities, runs experiments, and shapes roadmap with data. Closer to product and growth than to ML infrastructure.

roles.name: Marketing Data Scientist
roles.blurb: Applies data science to growth and marketing: attribution, media-mix modeling, LTV and churn prediction, and campaign experimentation. Balances causal rigor with fast, budget-moving decisions.

roles.name: Operations Research Scientist
roles.blurb: Optimizes complex operations: routing, scheduling, pricing, inventory, and supply chains using optimization and simulation. Turns business constraints into solvable math and measurable efficiency gains at logistics, airline, and marketplace companies.

roles.name: Bioinformatics Scientist
roles.blurb: Analyzes biological data at scale — genomics, proteomics, single-cell — building pipelines and statistical models to find signals in DNA and molecular data. Sits at the intersection of biology, statistics, and scientific computing.

roles.name: Causal Inference Scientist
roles.blurb: Specializes in the hardest question in data — what actually causes what — using quasi-experiments, uplift models, and observational-causal methods when clean A/B tests aren't possible. A rising, high-value niche across tech, health, and policy.

roles.name: Model Risk / Risk Quant Analyst
roles.blurb: Validates and governs the models a bank or insurer relies on: stress-tests assumptions, checks credit and market risk models, and keeps the firm defensible to regulators. Statistical rigor meets model governance and compliance.

roles.name: Survey Statistician
roles.blurb: Designs and analyzes surveys and census-style data: sampling frames, weighting, non-response adjustment, and error estimation. The backbone of official statistics, polling, and market research where representativeness matters.

roles.name: Machine Learning Engineer
roles.blurb: You take models from notebook to production, building training pipelines, features, and serving infra, then owning the model live as data drifts and metrics move. Half data scientist, half software engineer.

roles.name: AI Engineer
roles.blurb: You build product features on top of foundation models, wiring LLM APIs, retrieval, agents, and evals into real applications. Less model training, more systems, prompts, and shipping reliable AI UX.

roles.name: MLOps Engineer
roles.blurb: You build the paved road for ML: model registries, CI/CD for models, feature stores, and monitoring for drift and data quality. You keep training and serving reproducible and on-call-friendly.

roles.name: ML Platform Engineer
roles.blurb: You build the internal platform other ML teams build on: training orchestration, experiment tracking, pipelines, and self-serve tooling. Product engineering where your users are data scientists.

roles.name: ML Infrastructure Engineer
roles.blurb: You run the GPU fleets and distributed training stacks large models need: multi-node training, high-speed interconnects, scheduling, and squeezing utilization out of very expensive accelerators.

roles.name: Computer Vision Engineer
roles.blurb: You build systems that see: detection, segmentation, tracking, OCR, or 3D perception, from data collection and annotation through model training to real-time deployment on servers or edge devices.

roles.name: NLP Engineer
roles.blurb: You build language systems: classification, NER, information extraction, translation, and increasingly LLM-based pipelines. Text preprocessing, tokenization, and careful evaluation are your daily bread.

roles.name: Deep Learning Engineer
roles.blurb: You design, train, and tune neural networks, architectures, loss functions, and training regimes, for perception, language, or generative tasks. Deep in the math and staring at training curves.

roles.name: Recommender Systems Engineer
roles.blurb: You build the models that decide what users see next: candidate generation, ranking, embeddings, and real-time feature pipelines, optimizing engagement while fighting feedback loops and cold start.

roles.name: Search & Ranking Engineer
roles.blurb: You make search return the right thing: query understanding, retrieval, learning-to-rank, and relevance evaluation. Increasingly blends classic IR with embeddings and semantic vector search.

roles.name: ML Research Engineer
roles.blurb: You sit between research and production, implementing papers, running large-scale experiments, and building the tooling scientists need to iterate fast. Strong engineering, research literacy, GPU fluency.

roles.name: ML Research Scientist
roles.blurb: You do original research, novel architectures, training methods, or theory, publish at NeurIPS/ICML, and push the frontier. A PhD is expected; at frontier labs the comp and the compute are enormous.

roles.name: LLM Engineer
roles.blurb: You work directly on large language models: pretraining or fine-tuning, RLHF/DPO, data curation, tokenizers, and eval harnesses. Deep systems and ML skill, adjacent to frontier-model teams.

roles.name: Generative AI Engineer
roles.blurb: You build generative features, text, image, audio, or video, combining foundation models, fine-tuning, diffusion, and product engineering to ship creative and content tools people actually use.

roles.name: Prompt Engineer
roles.blurb: You get the most out of models without training them, designing prompts, building eval suites, and tuning system behavior for reliability, safety, and tone. Increasingly merges into AI engineering and product.

roles.name: Conversational AI Engineer
roles.blurb: You build chatbots and voice assistants, dialogue management, intent/NLU, and increasingly LLM-driven agents, wiring them into contact centers, apps, and support flows that actually resolve tasks.

roles.name: Speech & Audio ML Engineer
roles.blurb: You build systems that hear and speak: ASR, text-to-speech, speaker ID, and audio understanding. Signal processing meets deep learning, under tight latency and streaming constraints.

roles.name: Reinforcement Learning Engineer
roles.blurb: You train agents that learn from reward: RLHF for LLMs, control, robotics, or game AI. Reward design, simulation, and unstable training loops are the job; strong math and patience required.

roles.name: Ads ML Engineer
roles.blurb: You build the models behind ad auctions and targeting: CTR/CVR prediction, bidding, and budget pacing at massive scale. Small metric gains mean big revenue, so rigor and latency both matter.

roles.name: RAG / Applied LLM Engineer
roles.blurb: You ground LLMs in real data, building retrieval pipelines, chunking and embedding strategies, vector stores, and evals so answers are accurate and cited. The backbone of enterprise AI assistants.

roles.name: Inference Optimization Engineer
roles.blurb: You make models fast and cheap to run: quantization, kernel fusion, batching, and serving-engine tuning (vLLM/TensorRT). Every millisecond and every GPU-dollar of inference is your battlefield.

roles.name: Multimodal ML Engineer
roles.blurb: You build models that fuse modalities, vision-language, audio-text, or any-to-any, handling alignment, cross-modal training, and the messy data pipelines multimodal systems demand. Frontier territory.

roles.name: Edge / On-device ML Engineer
roles.blurb: You shrink models to run on phones, cameras, and microcontrollers, quantization, pruning, and hardware-aware optimization within tight memory, power, and latency budgets. Where ML meets embedded.

roles.name: GenAI Application Engineer
roles.blurb: Full-stack engineer who ships user-facing products powered by LLMs - chat, copilots, summarization - integrating model APIs, retrieval, and guardrails into real applications. The bread-and-butter builder role of the GenAI wave.

roles.name: AI Agent Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds autonomous and semi-autonomous agents that plan, call tools, and act - wiring reasoning loops, function calling, memory, and guardrails into multi-step workflows. One of the hottest and fastest-growing niches of 2025-2026.

roles.name: Forward-Deployed Engineer
roles.blurb: Embeds with customers to build and ship bespoke AI solutions on their data and systems - half engineer, half consultant, turning models into deployed value fast. Popularized by Palantir and now a marquee, high-comp role at frontier AI labs.

roles.name: AI Product Engineer
roles.blurb: Generalist who owns AI features end-to-end - from prototype to production - blending product intuition with engineering to ship LLM-powered experiences users love. Thrives in startups where one person carries a feature from idea to launch.

roles.name: AI Safety Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds the guardrails, filters, and safety evals that keep generative systems from producing harmful, biased, or unsafe outputs before and after deployment. Combines adversarial testing with policy and content-moderation work.

roles.name: AI Alignment Researcher
roles.blurb: Researches how to make advanced AI systems pursue intended goals - RLHF, interpretability, scalable oversight - usually at frontier labs, publishing and shaping how models are trained. A research-scientist track with top-of-market compensation.

roles.name: LLM Evaluation Engineer
roles.blurb: Designs the tests, benchmarks, and LLM-as-judge pipelines that measure model quality, catch regressions, and turn subjective 'is it good?' into reproducible metrics. The quality backbone that lets GenAI teams ship with confidence.

roles.name: AI Red Teamer
roles.blurb: Attacks AI systems on purpose - crafting jailbreaks, prompt injections, and adversarial inputs to surface harmful failures before real users or bad actors find them. Blends security mindset with deep knowledge of model behavior.

roles.name: LLMOps Engineer
roles.blurb: Runs LLMs in production - deployment, versioning, monitoring, cost and latency control, prompt and model-version management. The ops discipline that keeps GenAI apps reliable, observable, and affordable at scale.

roles.name: GenAI Solutions Architect
roles.blurb: Designs enterprise GenAI architectures - choosing models, retrieval patterns, and infra while balancing security, cost, and scale - and guides teams from proof-of-concept to production. Senior, cross-functional, and heavy on stakeholder work.

roles.name: Applied AI Research Engineer
roles.blurb: Bridges research and product - implementing papers, running experiments, and turning novel generative techniques into shippable capabilities within engineering teams. More hands-on than a pure researcher, more scientific than a product engineer.

roles.name: Fine-Tuning Engineer
roles.blurb: Adapts base models to domains and tasks - building training datasets, running LoRA/PEFT and full fine-tunes, and evaluating whether the tuned model actually beats the base. Deep on data curation and training mechanics.

roles.name: GenAI Product Manager
roles.blurb: Owns the what and why of AI products - scoping LLM features, defining evals and guardrails, managing model tradeoffs, and shipping generative experiences that deliver value. Needs genuine fluency in what models can and cannot do.

roles.name: RLHF Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds the human-feedback loops that align models - reward models, preference-data pipelines, and RL training that shape how LLMs respond to people. A specialized training role central to how modern assistants are made helpful and safe.

roles.name: LLM Inference Engineer
roles.blurb: Makes LLMs fast and cheap to run - serving stacks, quantization, batching, KV-cache and GPU-kernel optimization to squeeze tokens-per-second out of expensive hardware. Systems-heavy and carries a strong performance-engineering premium.

roles.name: Multimodal AI Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds systems that reason across text, images, audio, and video - integrating and fine-tuning multimodal models for search, generation, and understanding beyond plain text. Expanding fast as vision-language models mature.

roles.name: AI Automation Engineer
roles.blurb: Automates business processes with LLMs and agents - chaining tools, APIs, and no-code platforms to replace manual workflows with reliable AI-driven pipelines. Practical, integration-heavy, and increasingly in demand across ops teams.

roles.name: AI Solutions Engineer
roles.blurb: Customer-facing technical role - builds demos and POCs, scopes GenAI solutions, and helps prospects and customers succeed with LLM platforms, bridging sales and engineering. Comp blends base with meaningful variable pay.

roles.name: Data Analyst
roles.blurb: Turns raw business data into answers — writing SQL, cleaning messy tables, and building dashboards that tell stakeholders what happened and why. The bread-and-butter entry point into data careers; lots of ad-hoc requests, recurring reports, and translating vague questions into metrics.

roles.name: Business Intelligence Analyst
roles.blurb: Owns the reporting layer of the business — defining metrics, building governed dashboards, and making sure leaders trust the numbers. Sits between raw data and decision-makers, heavy on data modeling in the BI tool and on turning KPIs into a single source of truth.

roles.name: BI Developer
roles.blurb: The build side of business intelligence — engineering the ETL, semantic models, and report infrastructure that dashboards sit on. More technical and pipeline-focused than a BI analyst; you live in SQL, the data warehouse, and the BI platform's data layer rather than in stakeholder meetings.

roles.name: Product Analyst
roles.blurb: Embedded with a product team, measuring how users actually behave — funnels, retention, A/B tests, and feature adoption. You instrument events, define product metrics, and turn behavioral data into roadmap decisions. Sits close to PMs and often owns experimentation.

roles.name: Marketing Analyst
roles.blurb: Measures marketing performance — campaign ROI, attribution, channel spend, and customer acquisition cost. You pull from ad platforms and CRMs, build reporting for marketing leaders, and help decide where the budget goes. Blends analytics with a solid grasp of marketing funnels.

roles.name: Growth Analyst
roles.blurb: Analytics arm of a growth team — running experiments across acquisition, activation, and retention loops to move top-line metrics. More hypothesis-driven and full-funnel than a marketing analyst; you design tests, size opportunities, and obsess over conversion and LTV. Common at consumer and PLG startups.

stages.title: Growth Lead / Head of Growth Analytics

roles.name: Business Analyst
roles.blurb: The bridge between business stakeholders and delivery teams — eliciting requirements, mapping processes, and translating needs into specs, user stories, and reporting. In tech orgs it leans toward data and product; you spend as much time in stakeholder workshops as in spreadsheets. Ubiquitous and stable.

roles.name: Financial Analyst (Tech / FP&A)
roles.blurb: Financial planning and analysis inside a tech company — building models, forecasts, and budgets, and reporting on burn, revenue, and unit economics. Increasingly data-tool-heavy; you pair Excel modeling with SQL and BI to give finance leaders and the business real-time visibility.

roles.name: Reporting Analyst
roles.blurb: Owns recurring operational and regulatory reporting — building, running, and distributing the standard reports the business runs on. More production-and-accuracy focused than exploratory; heavy on SQL, spreadsheets, and BI templates. Increasingly automated, so the role is shifting toward self-serve enablement.

roles.name: Analytics Manager
roles.blurb: Leads a team of analysts — setting the analytics roadmap, managing stakeholders, and translating business strategy into measurable questions. Part people-manager, part senior analyst; you review work, prioritize requests, and make sure the team's output actually drives decisions. The management step above senior IC analysts.

roles.name: Tableau Developer
roles.blurb: Specialist who builds and optimizes Tableau dashboards and data sources at scale — LOD calculations, extracts, server publishing, and performance tuning. A tool-focused BI role common in enterprises with a big Tableau footprint. Steady demand, though Power BI has taken share of new deployments.

roles.name: Power BI Developer
roles.blurb: Builds enterprise reporting on the Microsoft stack — data models, DAX measures, and Power BI reports wired into the wider Azure/Fabric ecosystem. Strong, growing demand as Power BI dominates new BI rollouts. You live in DAX, Power Query, and semantic modeling.

roles.name: Data Visualization Specialist
roles.blurb: Focuses on how insight is communicated — designing clear, compelling dashboards, infographics, and interactive visualizations that non-analysts actually understand. Blends analytics with visual design and storytelling; often the person who makes executive reporting and public-facing data look sharp.

roles.name: Revenue Operations Analyst
roles.blurb: Analytics engine of the go-to-market org — reporting on pipeline, forecasting, quota attainment, and sales/marketing efficiency across the CRM and revenue stack. You keep Salesforce data clean, build the dashboards leadership runs the number on, and surface where deals leak. RevOps is one of the hotter analyst niches.

roles.name: Digital / Web Analytics Analyst
roles.blurb: Measures on-site and digital behavior — traffic, conversion, tagging, and attribution across GA4, tag managers, and testing tools. You own the analytics implementation as much as the reporting, and increasingly navigate privacy, consent, and cookieless measurement. Common in e-commerce and digital marketing teams.

roles.name: Operations Analyst
roles.blurb: Analyzes how the business runs day to day — throughput, SLAs, capacity, cost, and process efficiency across supply chain, support, or logistics. You find bottlenecks in operational data and recommend fixes. Practical and cross-functional, blending analytics with process improvement.

roles.name: Insights Analyst
roles.blurb: Synthesizes quantitative and qualitative data into narratives that shape strategy — combining behavioral data, surveys, and market research into 'so what' recommendations. More storytelling- and research-oriented than a pure reporting analyst; common in customer insights, market research, and consumer teams.

roles.name: DevOps Engineer
roles.blurb: You automate the path from code to production — building CI/CD pipelines, containerizing apps, and managing cloud infrastructure as code. Days mix pipeline debugging, on-call incident response, and cutting the toil out of deploys.

roles.name: Site Reliability Engineer
roles.blurb: You keep large-scale systems reliable — defining SLOs, running the on-call rotation, and engineering away the causes of outages. Half software engineering, half operations: you write code to eliminate toil and lead blameless postmortems when things break.

roles.name: Platform Engineer
roles.blurb: You build the internal platform other engineers ship on — golden paths, self-service infrastructure, and paved-road tooling that abstracts away Kubernetes and cloud plumbing. A product mindset applied to your own company's developers.

roles.name: Build & Release Engineer
roles.blurb: You own the machinery that turns source into shippable artifacts — build systems, versioning, and repeatable release pipelines. You keep builds fast, deterministic, and reproducible, and coordinate the mechanics of getting releases out the door.

roles.name: CI/CD Engineer
roles.blurb: You specialize in the continuous integration and delivery pipeline — wiring up automated builds, tests, and deployments so teams merge and ship many times a day. You fight flaky pipelines, slow builds, and manual release steps.

roles.name: Observability Engineer
roles.blurb: You make systems legible — instrumenting services with metrics, logs, and traces, and building the dashboards and alerts teams trust during incidents. You own the observability stack and help engineers actually understand what production is doing.

roles.name: Infrastructure Engineer
roles.blurb: You design, provision, and maintain the compute, network, and storage foundations everything runs on — mostly in the cloud, defined as code. You balance reliability, cost, and security while keeping the underlying infrastructure boring and dependable.

roles.name: Developer Experience Engineer
roles.blurb: Your customer is other engineers. You shave friction off their daily workflow — faster builds, smoother local setup, better tooling and docs — and measure success in developer productivity, not features shipped.

roles.name: Cloud Architect
roles.blurb: You design the cloud blueprint — which services, how they connect, how they scale, and what it costs — then guide teams through migrations and builds. Deeply technical but heavy on tradeoffs, stakeholder alignment, and long-horizon decisions.

roles.name: Kubernetes Engineer
roles.blurb: You live in Kubernetes — running production clusters, tuning workloads and networking, and building the GitOps and service-mesh layers around them. A deep container-orchestration specialist for organizations that run everything on k8s.

roles.name: DevSecOps Engineer
roles.blurb: You bake security into the delivery pipeline — automated scanning, secrets management, hardened containers, and policy as code — so teams ship fast without shipping vulnerabilities. Sits at the intersection of DevOps and application/cloud security.

roles.name: Production Engineer
roles.blurb: An SRE-style role (the Meta term) embedded with product teams — you own the reliability, scalability, and performance of specific systems, deep in the code and the on-call rotation. Software engineers who specialize in making services run well at scale.

roles.name: Systems Administrator
roles.blurb: You keep the servers, networks, and core IT services running — provisioning accounts, patching systems, handling backups, and fixing what breaks. The traditional ops backbone, increasingly automating itself toward cloud and DevOps work.

roles.name: Linux Systems Engineer
roles.blurb: You are the deep Linux specialist — tuning kernels, debugging performance, automating fleet configuration, and keeping thousands of hosts healthy. Where sysadmin work meets serious engineering and automation at scale.

roles.name: Release Manager
roles.blurb: You orchestrate how software gets to production across teams — planning release trains, gating quality, managing risk, and communicating go/no-go. Part engineering, part program management: the person who makes ship day predictable.

roles.name: Infrastructure Automation Engineer
roles.blurb: You turn manual infrastructure work into code — provisioning, configuration, and policy all automated and version-controlled. If a task is done twice by hand, you build the pipeline or module that does it a thousand times reliably.

roles.name: Chaos Engineer
roles.blurb: You deliberately break things to make them stronger — designing failure experiments, injecting faults, and proving systems survive the outages you simulate. A resilience specialty within SRE, turning 'what if this fails?' into evidence.

roles.name: Internal Tools Engineer
roles.blurb: You build the software your own company runs on internally — admin dashboards, operational tooling, and integrations that make other teams faster. Full-stack work with a captive user base and direct, visible impact on how the business operates.

roles.name: Platform Architect
roles.blurb: You set the technical direction for the internal platform — the architecture, standards, and long-term roadmap that dozens of teams build on. High-leverage, tradeoff-heavy work spanning cloud, Kubernetes, and organization-wide engineering strategy.

roles.name: Cloud Operations Engineer
roles.blurb: You run cloud environments day to day — watching dashboards, responding to alerts, managing cost and capacity, and keeping workloads healthy. The operations-focused counterpart to the cloud engineer, heavy on monitoring, response, and steady-state reliability.

roles.name: Cloud Engineer
roles.blurb: You build and operate the cloud environment day to day — provisioning infrastructure as code, wiring up networking and IAM, automating deploys, and keeping the lights on. It's a hands-on generalist role that sits between DevOps and traditional sysadmin, heavy on Terraform, scripting and one primary cloud.

roles.name: Solutions Architect
roles.blurb: You translate a customer's or business unit's requirements into a concrete technical solution, often in a presales or delivery-facing capacity. Half architecture, half consulting: whiteboarding designs, writing proposals, running proofs of concept, and being the technical voice in the room. Common at cloud vendors and consultancies.

roles.name: Systems Architect
roles.blurb: You own how the hardware, OS, virtualization and networking layers fit together into a coherent, reliable platform — often spanning on-prem and cloud. It's a deep-infrastructure role focused on availability, capacity and performance rather than application code, with a lot of design docs and standards-setting.

roles.name: Infrastructure Architect
roles.blurb: You set the blueprint for compute, storage, network and virtualization across the estate, deciding standards, reference designs and DR strategy. It bridges classic data-center architecture and cloud, and you spend your time on design reviews, roadmaps and making sure builds conform to the pattern.

roles.name: FinOps Engineer
roles.blurb: You make cloud spend visible and accountable — building cost dashboards, enforcing tagging, spotting waste, negotiating commitments (RIs/savings plans), and partnering with engineering and finance to forecast bills. A fast-emerging specialty that blends cloud engineering with financial analysis.

roles.name: Virtualization Engineer
roles.blurb: You run the hypervisor layer — building and maintaining VMware vSphere/ESXi (or Hyper-V) clusters, managing VMs, resource pools, HA/DRS and backups. Core to on-prem and private-cloud estates; steady but under pressure from cloud migration and Broadcom-era VMware licensing shifts.

roles.name: Storage Engineer
roles.blurb: You design and operate the storage tier — SAN/NAS arrays, block/object/file, replication and backup — sizing capacity and IOPS and keeping data durable and fast. Deep hardware-and-protocol knowledge (NetApp, Dell EMC, Pure, fibre channel) with a growing cloud-storage dimension.

roles.name: AWS Solutions Architect
roles.blurb: An AWS-specialized architect — you design workloads against the Well-Architected Framework, choosing the right mix of EC2, S3, VPC, Lambda, RDS and more, and often carry the AWS SA-Pro certification. Split between building reference architectures and advising teams or customers on the AWS-native way to do things.

roles.name: Azure Cloud Engineer
roles.blurb: You build and run workloads on Microsoft Azure — provisioning via ARM/Bicep or Terraform, wiring up VNets, Entra ID and AKS, and integrating with the wider Microsoft stack. Strong demand in enterprise and public-sector shops that are Microsoft-first.

roles.name: GCP Cloud Architect
roles.blurb: A Google Cloud-specialized architect — you design on GCP's building blocks (GKE, BigQuery, Cloud Run, VPC) and are often the go-to for data- and Kubernetes-heavy workloads. Common at data-forward and ML-forward orgs, carrying the Professional Cloud Architect cert.

roles.name: Enterprise Architect
roles.blurb: You own the top-level technology strategy across the whole business — aligning application, data and infrastructure roadmaps to business goals, setting standards and governance, and guiding major investments. Very senior and strategic, often TOGAF-framed, with more time in exec conversations than in a console.

roles.name: Cloud Infrastructure Engineer
roles.blurb: You own the cloud plumbing — networking, compute, IAM, Kubernetes and the IaC pipelines that provision it all — as reusable, self-service platform. Closer to platform/DevOps than app development, heavy on Terraform, automation and reliability.

roles.name: Cloud Security Architect
roles.blurb: You design the security posture of the cloud estate — IAM and identity, network segmentation, encryption, guardrails, zero-trust and compliance controls — and set the patterns engineers must follow. A high-premium specialty blending security architecture with deep cloud-platform knowledge.

roles.name: Cloud Network Engineer
roles.blurb: You design and run the network fabric in the cloud — VPC/VNet architecture, routing, peering, transit gateways, firewalls, VPN and hybrid connectivity to on-prem. A networking specialist adapting classic CCNP-style skills to software-defined cloud networking.

roles.name: Cloud Migration Engineer
roles.blurb: You move workloads from on-prem or one cloud to another — assessing the estate, planning the wave, rehosting/replatforming apps and databases, and running cutovers with minimal downtime. Project-driven and pattern-heavy, using tools like AWS MGN, Azure Migrate and lots of scripting.

roles.name: Cloud Consultant
roles.blurb: You advise clients on cloud strategy, architecture, migration and cost — usually from a consultancy or systems integrator, jumping across engagements. Part architect, part project delivery, part relationship management, with breadth across multiple providers valued over depth in one.

roles.name: Data Center Engineer
roles.blurb: You keep physical infrastructure running — racking and cabling servers, managing power, cooling and network gear, and handling hardware faults on the floor. Hands-on and shift-oriented; seeing a resurgence with the AI-driven data-center buildout even as generic on-prem shrinks.

roles.name: Hybrid Cloud Engineer
roles.blurb: You stitch on-prem and public cloud into one operating model — extending VMware/private estates into AWS/Azure, managing connectivity, identity and workload placement across both, often via platforms like Azure Arc or VMware Cloud. For orgs that can't or won't go all-in on public cloud.

roles.name: CloudOps Engineer
roles.blurb: You operate cloud environments in production — monitoring and observability, incident response, patching, cost hygiene and keeping automation running. Focused on run/operate rather than build, sitting between SRE and traditional operations with a strong on-call component.

roles.name: Security Engineer
roles.blurb: Broad defender role: build and harden the controls that protect systems, review architectures for weaknesses, run vulnerability management, and respond when something breaks. Half engineering, half detective work across cloud, network, and app layers.

roles.name: Application Security Engineer
roles.blurb: Shifts security left into the SDLC: reviews code and designs for flaws, runs SAST/DAST tooling, triages bug-bounty reports, and coaches developers on secure patterns. You live where software engineering meets attack surface.

roles.name: Product Security Engineer
roles.blurb: Owns the security of a specific product or platform end to end: threat models new features, drives secure-by-default design, hunts for vulns in the codebase, and partners tightly with product engineering teams. Deeper product context than a generalist AppSec role.

roles.name: Penetration Tester
roles.blurb: Paid to break in: run scoped, time-boxed assessments against web apps, networks, and cloud, chain vulnerabilities into real impact, and write it all up for the client. Fast-paced, project-based, heavy on hands-on exploitation and clear reporting.

roles.name: Red Team Operator
roles.blurb: Emulates real adversaries over long engagements: builds custom tooling and C2 infrastructure, evades EDR, moves laterally through AD, and tests whether the blue team can actually detect a determined attacker. Stealth and OPSEC matter as much as exploitation.

roles.name: SOC Analyst
roles.blurb: Front line of the blue team: monitors alerts in the SIEM, triages and escalates incidents, and hunts through logs and EDR telemetry, often on shifts. High-volume, high-learning entry point into security — the tier where automation and AI are reshaping the job most.

roles.name: GRC Analyst
roles.blurb: Governance, risk, and compliance: maps controls to frameworks like ISO 27001 and SOC 2, runs risk assessments and audits, writes policy, and shepherds evidence for certifications. Documentation- and stakeholder-heavy rather than hands-on-keyboard hacking.

roles.name: Cloud Security Engineer
roles.blurb: Secures AWS/Azure/GCP estates at scale: hardens IAM and network config, deploys CSPM/CNAPP guardrails, bakes security into Terraform and Kubernetes, and chases misconfigurations before attackers do. One of the fastest-growing, best-paid security specialties.

roles.name: DFIR Analyst
roles.blurb: Digital forensics and incident response: when a breach hits, you scope it, pull and analyze memory/disk/log evidence, figure out how the attacker got in and what they touched, and drive containment and recovery. High-adrenaline, deadline-driven investigative work.

roles.name: Security Architect
roles.blurb: Designs the security blueprint for the whole organization: sets standards, defines zero-trust and IAM patterns, reviews major system designs, and balances risk against business needs. Senior, influence-heavy role that shapes decisions rather than shipping code daily.

roles.name: IAM Engineer
roles.blurb: Owns identity and access: runs SSO/SAML/OIDC, provisioning, lifecycle, and privileged access across the org's apps and directories. Quietly critical plumbing work — get it wrong and everyone's locked out or everyone's over-permissioned.

roles.name: Malware Analyst / Reverse Engineer
roles.blurb: Tears apart malicious binaries to understand what they do: static and dynamic analysis in IDA/Ghidra, unpacking and deobfuscation, and writing detection signatures. Deep, patient, low-level work for people who enjoy reading disassembly.

roles.name: Threat Intelligence Analyst
roles.blurb: Tracks the adversaries: profiles threat actors and campaigns, mines OSINT and dark-web sources, produces IOCs and actionable reports, and briefs defenders on what's coming. Part analyst, part researcher, part writer.

roles.name: Information Security Analyst
roles.blurb: The broad, generalist security seat many orgs hire first: monitors for threats, runs vulnerability scans, supports audits, and helps with incident handling and awareness. Wide-but-shallow exposure that's a common launchpad into deeper specialties.

roles.name: Chief Information Security Officer
roles.blurb: The executive who owns security risk for the whole company: sets strategy and budget, runs the security org, answers to the board and regulators, and is on the hook when a breach makes the news. Leadership and communication far more than hands-on tech.

roles.name: Security Consultant
roles.blurb: Advisory work across many clients: runs security assessments, gap analyses against frameworks, and remediation roadmaps, then presents findings to stakeholders. Variety and travel, strong communication, and a fast track to broad exposure.

roles.name: Vulnerability Researcher
roles.blurb: Finds new, unknown vulnerabilities in software and hardware: reverse engineering, fuzzing at scale, and writing proof-of-concept exploits. Elite, low-headcount, well-paid work that overlaps bug-bounty, product security, and offensive research.

roles.name: Detection Engineer
roles.blurb: Builds the detections the SOC runs on: writes and tunes Sigma/YARA/SIEM rules, maps coverage to ATT&CK, engineers log pipelines, and reduces false positives. Where security meets data engineering — a fast-rising specialty.

roles.name: Threat Hunter
roles.blurb: Proactively hunts for attackers already inside the environment, without waiting for an alert: forms hypotheses from ATT&CK and intel, digs through EDR and log telemetry, and turns findings into new detections. Curious, analytical, senior blue-team work.

roles.name: Cryptography Engineer
roles.blurb: Applies cryptography in production: designs and implements protocols, key management, and PKI, reviews crypto for correctness, and increasingly leads post-quantum migrations. Rare, math-heavy, and highly paid — small mistakes have big blast radius.

roles.name: OT / ICS Security Engineer
roles.blurb: Secures industrial and critical-infrastructure systems — SCADA, PLCs, and OT networks in factories, utilities, and plants — where availability and safety trump patching. Specialized niche with real supply-demand imbalance and rising regulatory pressure.

stages.title: Principal OT Security Engineer / ICS Security Architect

roles.name: Security Engineering Manager
roles.blurb: Leads a team of security engineers: sets the roadmap, hires and grows people, runs the program, and translates between technical risk and business priorities. Still close enough to the tech to be credible, but the job is people and delivery.

roles.name: Network Engineer
roles.blurb: Designs, configures, and maintains the routers, switches, and firewalls that keep an organization's LAN and WAN running. Days mix change windows, troubleshooting outages by tracing packets and BGP/OSPF adjacencies, and steady capacity and lifecycle work.

roles.name: Network Architect
roles.blurb: Owns the high-level design of enterprise and cloud networks — topology, routing strategy, segmentation, and resilience — then hands runbooks to the engineers who build it. Heavy on whiteboarding, vendor evaluation, and translating business needs into standards.

roles.name: IT Support Specialist / Help Desk
roles.blurb: The first line when something breaks — resetting accounts, chasing tickets, walking users through fixes, and escalating what can't be solved at the desk. High volume, customer-facing, and the classic entry door into IT.

roles.name: Desktop Support Technician
roles.blurb: Hands-on end-user support — imaging laptops, swapping hardware, deploying software, and fixing whatever won't work at someone's desk. More physical and on-site than remote help desk, and a common step toward endpoint and infra roles.

roles.name: Endpoint Engineer
roles.blurb: Manages the fleet at scale — Intune/SCCM policies, Autopilot provisioning, patch rings, and app packaging across thousands of Windows and Mac devices. Growing fast as zero-trust and modern management replace hands-on desktop work.

roles.name: Telecom Engineer
roles.blurb: Provisions and maintains the voice and circuit infrastructure — PBXs, carrier links, cabling, and the SIP trunks that carry calls. A mix of physical plant work and troubleshooting across carrier boundaries.

roles.name: VoIP Engineer
roles.blurb: Runs the IP telephony backbone — CUCM/CallManager, session border controllers, QoS, and codec tuning so voice traffic stays clean under load. Deep packet-capture debugging when calls drop or one-way audio strikes.

roles.name: Unified Communications Engineer
roles.blurb: Owns the collaboration stack — Teams, Cisco UC, video rooms, and contact-center voice — tying telephony, meetings, and messaging into one experience. Part voice engineering, part cloud platform administration.

roles.name: Wireless Network Engineer
roles.blurb: Designs and tunes WLANs — site surveys, AP placement, channel and power plans, and chasing roaming and interference problems. Rising demand as Wi-Fi 6/7 and private 5G push more workloads onto the air.

roles.name: RF Engineer
roles.blurb: Works the physics of wireless — propagation modeling, antenna and link-budget design, spectrum analysis, and drive testing for cellular, 5G, and satellite networks. Often an EE-heavy role sitting between telecom carriers and hardware.

roles.name: Datacenter Technician
roles.blurb: The hands in the building — racking and cabling servers, swapping failed drives and DIMMs, running smart-hands tickets, and keeping power and cooling zones tidy. One of the fastest-growing roles as AI buildouts fill new datacenters.

roles.name: NOC Engineer
roles.blurb: Watches the network from the operations center — monitoring dashboards, triaging alerts, opening carrier tickets, and driving incident bridges around the clock. Shift-based and fast-paced, a strong launchpad into network engineering.

roles.name: Network Automation Engineer
roles.blurb: Replaces hand-typed CLI with code — Python, Ansible, and CI/CD pipelines that push and validate config across the fleet. The bridge between traditional networking and DevOps, and one of the highest-growth niches in infra.

roles.name: Field Service Technician
roles.blurb: On the road installing, repairing, and decommissioning IT and network gear across client sites — cabling, hardware swaps, and on-site troubleshooting. Independent, customer-facing work with a lot of windshield time.

roles.name: IT Operations Manager
roles.blurb: Runs the IT service and infrastructure function — leading support and ops teams, owning SLAs, vendors, budgets, and the incident/change process. Less hands-on-keyboard, more people, process, and keeping the lights on for the business.

roles.name: Network Security Engineer
roles.blurb: Secures the network perimeter and core — firewalls, VPNs, IDS/IPS, segmentation, and zero-trust access — and hunts down what gets through. Sits at the intersection of networking and security, and commands a clear pay premium.

roles.name: QA Engineer
roles.blurb: Owns quality for a product area — writes and runs test cases, files and verifies bugs, and increasingly automates regression suites. A blend of hands-on functional testing, exploratory work, and light scripting alongside developers in an agile team.

roles.name: Software Development Engineer in Test (SDET)
roles.blurb: A software engineer who builds the tooling and automation that verifies other engineers' code — frameworks, harnesses, CI test infrastructure, and complex end-to-end suites. Codes to production standards, so pay tracks close to a regular SWE.

roles.name: Test Automation Engineer
roles.blurb: Designs and maintains automated test frameworks and scripts that replace repetitive manual regression. Lives in Selenium/Cypress/Playwright, wires suites into CI pipelines, and keeps flaky tests and reporting under control.

roles.name: Performance / Load Test Engineer
roles.blurb: Specializes in how systems behave under load — designs load, stress, and soak tests, profiles bottlenecks, and works with engineers to tune throughput and latency. A niche, well-paid corner of testing that overlaps with performance engineering.

roles.name: Manual QA Tester
roles.blurb: Executes test cases by hand, explores the product to find defects code paths miss, and documents clear reproduction steps. Still essential for UX-heavy and edge-case work, but a role under pressure as automation and AItesting absorb routine regression.

roles.name: QA Lead
roles.blurb: The senior IC/player-coach who owns test strategy for a team — decides what and how to test, reviews automation, runs release quality gates, and mentors testers. Balances hands-on work with planning and stakeholder communication.

roles.name: Quality Assurance Manager
roles.blurb: Owns the QA function — process, tooling strategy, headcount, and quality metrics across teams. A people-management role focused on building the testing org, driving automation adoption, and being accountable for release quality to the business.

roles.name: Game QA Tester
roles.blurb: Plays builds to break them — hunts gameplay, graphics, and crash bugs, writes tight repro steps, and runs regression and compliance passes across consoles, PC, and mobile. A passion-driven entry point into games that is notoriously low-paid and crunch-prone.

roles.name: QA Analyst
roles.blurb: Bridges requirements and testing — analyzes specs, designs functional test cases, and validates that the build meets business needs, often coordinating UAT. More analysis-and-documentation heavy than code-heavy, common in enterprise and finance shops.

roles.name: Mobile QA Engineer
roles.blurb: Specializes in testing iOS and Android apps across a fragmented matrix of devices, OS versions, and network conditions. Combines device-lab and emulator work with Appium/Espresso/XCUITest automation and debugging of platform-specific quirks.

roles.name: API Test Engineer
roles.blurb: Focuses on the layer below the UI — validates REST/GraphQL contracts, integration flows, and back-end services with automated checks in Postman, RestAssured, or code. Strong on scripting and data, weak on clicking through screens.

roles.name: Test Architect
roles.blurb: The most senior technical voice on quality — designs the automation strategy, frameworks, and tooling that scale across many teams, and sets standards for CI, test data, and coverage. A hands-on-but-strategic role that pays like a staff/principal engineer.

roles.name: Accessibility Test Engineer
roles.blurb: Verifies that products work for people using assistive technology — audits against WCAG, tests with screen readers and keyboard-only flows, and pairs automated scans with manual judgment. A growing specialty pushed by ADA, Section 508, and the EU EAA.

roles.name: Game QA Lead
roles.blurb: Runs the QA effort on a title — plans test coverage, triages the bug database, manages a team of testers, and shepherds console certification and compliance passes toward ship. More responsibility than a tester, but still below general-tech leads on pay.

roles.name: Localization QA Tester (LQA)
roles.blurb: Tests localized builds for linguistic and cultural correctness — catches mistranslations, truncated strings, layout breaks, and region-specific issues across many languages. Requires native-level fluency and a sharp eye for in-context UI detail.

roles.name: Product Manager
roles.blurb: Owns the what and why of a product area: talks to users, defines the roadmap, writes specs, and rallies engineering, design and go-to-market around a shared bet. Days are a blend of customer calls, prioritization tradeoffs, and unblocking the team.

roles.name: Associate Product Manager
roles.blurb: The entry point into product: shadows senior PMs, owns small features end to end, runs research and analysis, and learns to translate user problems into shipped software. Often a structured rotational program at larger tech companies.

roles.name: Senior Product Manager
roles.blurb: Runs a meaningful product area with autonomy, sets the strategy for it, and is measured on business outcomes rather than shipped features. Spends less time on execution mechanics and more on framing the right problems and influencing across teams.

roles.name: Technical Product Manager
roles.blurb: A PM for deeply technical products — APIs, infrastructure, developer tools — who can go toe to toe with engineers on architecture and tradeoffs. Balances technical depth with user and business framing, often coming from an engineering background.

roles.name: Group Product Manager
roles.blurb: Leads a cluster of PMs and their product areas, owning strategy for a whole domain while managing and coaching the individual PMs under them. The first real people-leadership rung on the product track — part strategist, part manager.

roles.name: Principal Product Manager
roles.blurb: The senior individual-contributor track: owns the hardest, most ambiguous, highest-leverage product problems without managing people. Drives cross-org strategy through influence and deep product judgment rather than headcount.

roles.name: Director of Product Management
roles.blurb: Owns product strategy and outcomes for a whole product line or business unit, managing a team of PMs and GPMs. Accountable for hiring, prioritization across the portfolio, and translating company strategy into product bets.

roles.name: VP of Product
roles.blurb: The senior product executive for a company or major division: sets the multi-year product vision, builds and leads the PM org, and sits at the table for company strategy alongside engineering and go-to-market leaders. Heavily cross-functional and business-outcome driven.

roles.name: Chief Product Officer
roles.blurb: The top product role, owning the entire product function and its strategy at the executive/C-suite level. Sets the vision, builds the leadership bench, and answers to the CEO and board for the product's contribution to company success.

roles.name: Product Owner
roles.blurb: The agile-execution counterpart to a PM: owns and grooms the backlog, writes user stories, and represents the customer inside the scrum team day to day. Heavier on delivery and sprint mechanics, lighter on market strategy — common in enterprises running SAFe/Scrum.

roles.name: Growth Product Manager
roles.blurb: A PM obsessed with the funnel — acquisition, activation, retention, monetization — who ships a constant stream of experiments to move metrics. Lives in analytics and A/B tests, partnering tightly with data, marketing and engineering.

roles.name: Platform Product Manager
roles.blurb: Owns internal or external platforms — shared services, SDKs, developer APIs — whose customers are often other engineering teams. Balances long-horizon technical investments against the needs of teams building on top, with success measured in adoption and leverage.

roles.name: Data Product Manager
roles.blurb: A PM for data as a product — pipelines, warehouses, metrics layers, internal data platforms, or customer-facing analytics. Bridges data engineering, analytics and business users, and is fluent in the tradeoffs of data quality, governance and modeling.

roles.name: AI Product Manager
roles.blurb: Owns products built on machine learning and LLMs — defining use cases, curating data and evals, and shipping model-powered features while managing the probabilistic, non-deterministic nature of AI. One of the fastest-growing and best-paid PM specializations.

roles.name: Product Operations Manager
roles.blurb: Builds the systems and rituals that make the product org run — planning cadences, tooling, metrics dashboards, customer-feedback pipelines, and cross-team communication. Force-multiplies the PM team so PMs can focus on product rather than process.

roles.name: API Product Manager
roles.blurb: Treats APIs as first-class products whose users are developers: owns the interface design, documentation, versioning, and developer experience, and grows adoption across the ecosystem. Sits at the intersection of engineering, partnerships and DX.

roles.name: Payments Product Manager
roles.blurb: Owns payment and fintech products — checkout, wallets, payouts, ledgers — where correctness, regulation and fraud risk are as important as user experience. Deep domain knowledge of payment rails, compliance and money movement is the price of entry.

roles.name: Security Product Manager
roles.blurb: Owns security and compliance products or the security posture of a product line — authentication, access control, threat detection, enterprise trust features. Translates a complex threat landscape and enterprise buyer requirements into a shippable roadmap.

roles.name: Product Designer
roles.blurb: Owns the end-to-end experience of a product area: framing the problem, sketching flows, building interactive Figma prototypes, and shipping polished UI alongside engineers and a PM. Balances user needs, business goals, and technical constraints, and is expected to defend decisions with research and metrics.

roles.name: UX Designer
roles.blurb: Focuses on the structure and usability of an experience — turning research and requirements into flows, wireframes, and testable prototypes. Often works upstream of visual polish, mapping how people move through a product and validating that it makes sense before it gets built.

roles.name: UI Designer
roles.blurb: Crafts the visual surface of digital products — layout, type, color, spacing, states, and pixel-level polish — usually working from flows a UX or product designer has defined. Increasingly folded into the broader product-designer role, but still hired as a distinct craft-focused title at agencies and larger orgs.

roles.name: UX Researcher
roles.blurb: Plans and runs studies — interviews, usability tests, surveys, diary studies — to answer what users need and where products fail them, then synthesizes findings into decisions teams act on. Mixes qualitative rigor with enough quant to size problems and persuade stakeholders.

roles.name: Design Systems Designer
roles.blurb: Builds and maintains the shared component library, tokens, and usage guidelines that keep a product's UI consistent at scale. Sits between design and engineering, obsessing over reusability, accessibility, and documentation so dozens of teams ship from one source of truth.

roles.name: Interaction Designer
roles.blurb: Specializes in how a product behaves — the timing, transitions, states, gestures, and micro-interactions that make an interface feel responsive and understandable. Prototypes motion and behavior closely with engineers, focusing on the moment-to-moment feel rather than static screens.

roles.name: Service Designer
roles.blurb: Designs whole services across channels and touchpoints — not just screens but the front-stage and back-stage processes, staff, and systems that deliver value over time. Uses blueprints and journey maps to fix experiences that span apps, call centers, physical spaces, and org silos. Common in gov, health, banking, and telco.

roles.name: Content Designer / UX Writer
roles.blurb: Designs the words in a product — labels, buttons, error messages, onboarding, empty states — so the interface is clear, consistent, and on-voice. Works structurally alongside designers and PMs, not as a copywriter bolted on at the end, and increasingly owns content strategy and IA for their surface.

roles.name: Design Manager
roles.blurb: Leads a team of designers — hiring, coaching, running critiques, and unblocking work — while staying close enough to the craft to raise the quality bar. Trades hands-on pixels for people and process, translating product strategy into team priorities and growing individual careers.

stages.title: VP of Design / Head of Design

roles.name: Motion Designer
roles.blurb: Brings interfaces and brand to life through animation — loading states, transitions, onboarding sequences, product marketing, and explainer content. Lives in After Effects and increasingly in Figma and Lottie, handing off motion that engineers can implement faithfully.

roles.name: Visual Designer
roles.blurb: Owns the aesthetic craft — composition, typography, color, imagery, and visual hierarchy — across products, marketing, and brand touchpoints. Distinct from UI in that the remit often spans beyond the app into campaigns and identity, focused on making things look and feel deliberate and premium.

roles.name: UX Engineer
