roles.blurb: A hybrid who bridges design and front-end engineering — building production-grade UI, prototypes, and design-system components in real code. Fluent enough in design to make craft calls and fluent enough in React/CSS to ship them, they turn high-fidelity intent into what users actually touch.

roles.name: Lead Product Designer
roles.blurb: A senior individual contributor who sets design direction across a product area and mentors other designers without formally managing them. Owns the hardest, most ambiguous problems, aligns cross-functional partners on vision, and keeps craft and consistency high across multiple teams.

roles.name: Design Director
roles.blurb: Leads design for a whole product line or business unit — usually managing managers — and owns the vision, standards, and staffing behind it. Operates at the intersection of design, product, and business strategy, answering to executives while protecting the team's craft and headcount.

roles.name: Brand Designer
roles.blurb: Shapes how a company looks and feels — logo systems, identity, color and type, illustration, and the visual voice across product, marketing, and social. Balances creative art direction with the discipline of a scalable, consistent brand system that non-designers can apply.

roles.name: Accessibility Specialist
roles.blurb: Makes products usable by everyone — auditing against WCAG, testing with screen readers and assistive tech, and coaching designers and engineers on inclusive patterns. Increasingly in demand as legal mandates (ADA, EAA) turn accessibility from nice-to-have into compliance requirement.

roles.name: DesignOps Manager
roles.blurb: Runs the operating system of a design org — tooling, rituals, onboarding, budgets, workflows, and metrics — so designers can focus on designing. A newer, growing discipline that scales design teams without scaling chaos, owning everything from Figma licensing to hiring pipelines.

roles.name: Conversation Designer
roles.blurb: Designs how people talk to software — chatbots, voice assistants, and increasingly LLM-powered agents — crafting dialogue flows, intents, tone, and error recovery. Blends UX writing, interaction design, and a working grasp of NLU and prompting; demand is climbing fast with the AI-assistant wave.

roles.name: Information Architect
roles.blurb: Organizes content and functionality so people can find and understand it — taxonomies, navigation, labeling, and content models behind large sites, apps, and knowledge bases. A structural, systems-minded craft that becomes critical as products and content libraries grow complex.

roles.name: VP of Design
roles.blurb: The executive who owns design across an entire company — vision, culture, org structure, and a seat at the strategy table. Builds and represents the design function to the C-suite and board, hires the leadership beneath them, and ties design outcomes to business results. A rare, high-leverage role.

roles.name: Engineering Manager
roles.blurb: Runs a team of 5-8 engineers: 1:1s, career growth, hiring, and shipping the roadmap. You trade most of your coding time for unblocking people, managing delivery, and translating between execs and engineers.

roles.name: Senior Engineering Manager
roles.blurb: Owns a larger area, often managing a couple of teams or a mix of ICs and team leads. The work is scaling, cross-team delivery, and org health more than individual coaching.

roles.name: Director of Engineering
roles.blurb: Manages managers and owns a department's strategy, budget, and delivery. Days are org design, hiring leaders, executive alignment, and rarely touching code.

roles.name: VP of Engineering
roles.blurb: Leads an entire engineering organization: strategy, org structure, senior hiring, and execution at scale. You own outcomes and budget, and spend most time with peers in product, sales, and the exec team.

roles.name: Chief Technology Officer (CTO)
roles.blurb: Sets the company's technology strategy and owns the engineering org top to bottom. At startups it's hands-on architecture and hiring; at scale it's vision, org building, and representing tech to the board and market.

stages.title: VP of Engineering / Head of Engineering

roles.name: Lead Software Engineer
roles.blurb: A hands-on senior engineer who leads delivery for a small group, owning a service or product area end to end. Heavier on coding than an EM, lighter on people process than a manager.

roles.name: Distinguished Engineer
roles.blurb: A rare, company-wide technical authority setting direction across the whole business. You shape multi-year architecture bets, represent the company's engineering externally, and mentor principals.

roles.name: Technical Fellow
roles.blurb: The most senior IC title that exists, held by a handful of people per company. You set the technical agenda for the entire firm, drive deep research, and are recognized industry-wide as a leader in your field.

roles.name: Head of Platform Engineering
roles.blurb: Owns the internal platform, developer experience, and infrastructure that every product team builds on. You balance reliability, cost, and velocity, and lead the teams behind CI/CD, cloud, and tooling.

roles.name: Head of Engineering
roles.blurb: The top engineering leader at a startup or scaleup, often below a CTO or wearing both hats. You build and scale the team, own delivery, and set process while staying close enough to the code to make calls.

roles.name: Chief Architect
roles.blurb: Owns the technical architecture and standards for an entire organization or enterprise. You set the reference architectures, govern technology choices, and align many teams and architects behind one coherent design.

roles.name: Embedded Systems Engineer
roles.blurb: You write firmware and low-level software that runs directly on microcontrollers and SoCs — often bare-metal or on an RTOS, with tight memory and timing budgets. The work mixes C, datasheets, oscilloscopes, and debugging why a device hangs after three days in the field.

roles.name: Firmware Engineer
roles.blurb: You own the code that boots a device and mediates between silicon and the rest of the stack — bootloaders, drivers, power management, OTA update paths. Success is measured in reliability, boot time, and battery life, and a bad flash can brick hardware in a customer's hands.

roles.name: Robotics Engineer
roles.blurb: You build the software that makes machines perceive and move — motion planning, control loops, sensor fusion, and the ROS graph that ties it together. The work spans simulation and real hardware, and the hardest bugs live in the gap between the two.

roles.name: Controls / Motion Control Engineer
roles.blurb: You design and tune the feedback systems that keep motors, actuators, and mechatronic systems stable and precise — PID loops, state-space controllers, real-time control on motion hardware. Half the job is math and modeling, the other half is bench work chasing latency and resonance.

roles.name: Game Engine Programmer
roles.blurb: You build and extend the engine itself — the rendering, physics, memory, and gameplay systems that a whole studio builds on top of. Performance is the product: you live in profilers, cache lines, and frame budgets measured in milliseconds.

roles.name: Graphics / Rendering Engineer
roles.blurb: You write the code that turns geometry into pixels — shaders, rendering pipelines, lighting and materials on Vulkan, DirectX, or Metal. The work is deeply GPU-aware, part visual craft and part squeezing every last microsecond out of the hardware.

roles.name: Blockchain Engineer
roles.blurb: You build decentralized systems — protocol-level infrastructure, nodes, wallets, and the backend that connects apps to chains. You reason about consensus, cryptography, and adversarial economics, because in this domain every bug is potentially a live exploit with money on the line.

roles.name: Smart Contract Engineer
roles.blurb: You write and audit the on-chain code that holds value — DeFi protocols, tokens, and governance logic in Solidity or Rust. The bar is unforgiving: contracts are immutable once deployed, so you obsess over gas, reentrancy, and formal correctness before anything ships.

roles.name: AR/VR/XR Engineer
roles.blurb: You build immersive experiences for headsets and mobile AR — spatial tracking, hand and eye input, and rendering that has to hit 90fps or players get sick. The work fuses 3D graphics, real-time engines, and a hard constraint on comfort and latency.

roles.name: Quantum Computing Engineer
roles.blurb: You develop quantum algorithms and the software that controls qubits — circuits, error mitigation, and the classical stack that orchestrates it all. It's a research-heavy field where a physics fluency and a software craft meet, and most of the hardware is still noisy and early.

roles.name: Bioinformatics Engineer
roles.blurb: You build the pipelines and tooling that turn raw genomic and biological data into analyzable results — sequence alignment, variant calling, and reproducible workflows at scale. You sit between wet-lab biology and large-scale compute, and correctness matters because results drive research and diagnostics.

roles.name: FPGA / Hardware Design Engineer
roles.blurb: You describe digital hardware in RTL — Verilog or VHDL — and coax it through synthesis, timing closure, and on-chip verification. The work is unforgiving about clock domains and timing, and a single metastable path can make a design fail intermittently in ways software never would.

roles.name: ASIC / Design Verification Engineer
roles.blurb: You prove that a chip design works before it's ever fabricated — building testbenches, coverage models, and constrained-random stimulus in SystemVerilog/UVM. Silicon respins cost millions, so your job is to find the bug now, in simulation, not after tape-out.

roles.name: Database Administrator (DBA)
roles.blurb: You keep the databases healthy, fast, and recoverable — tuning queries, planning capacity, managing backups and replication, and being the person who gets paged when the primary goes down. Increasingly the role blends classic admin with cloud-managed and reliability-engineering work.

roles.name: SAP Consultant / ERP Engineer
roles.blurb: You configure and extend SAP to run a company's core operations — finance, supply chain, HR — customizing modules and writing ABAP or building on S/4HANA and BTP. Deep domain knowledge of business processes matters as much as code, and migrations are long, high-stakes programs.

roles.name: Salesforce Developer
roles.blurb: You build on the Salesforce platform — Apex, Lightning Web Components, flows, and integrations that turn the CRM into custom business apps. The work is fast-moving and configuration-heavy, balancing declarative tools against real code and living inside platform governor limits.

roles.name: ServiceNow Developer
roles.blurb: You build workflows and applications on the ServiceNow platform — ITSM, ITOM, and custom modules that automate how enterprises run their internal operations. It's a niche, well-paid platform skill mixing JavaScript, low-code configuration, and process design.

roles.name: RPA / Automation Developer
roles.blurb: You automate repetitive business processes with tools like UiPath, Automation Anywhere, or Power Automate — building bots that click through legacy systems and stitch tasks together. Increasingly the role folds in AI and low-code, moving from screen-scraping bots toward intelligent orchestration.

roles.name: Low-Code Developer
roles.blurb: You build business applications on low-code platforms like Power Apps, OutSystems, or Mendix — assembling data models, logic, and UIs visually, dropping into code only where you must. It's a pragmatic, delivery-focused role that trades deep engineering for speed and business alignment.

roles.name: GIS Engineer / Geospatial Developer
roles.blurb: You build the systems that store, process, and visualize location data — spatial databases, mapping APIs, and pipelines that crunch satellite or sensor feeds. The work blends software engineering with cartography and geodesy, and it's growing fast on the back of drones, climate, and logistics.

roles.name: Simulation / CAE Engineer
roles.blurb: You model physical reality in software — running FEA, CFD, and multiphysics simulations to predict how designs behave before anything is built. You script and automate the tools, wrangle huge meshes on HPC clusters, and translate numerical results into engineering decisions.

roles.name: DSP / Audio Software Engineer
roles.blurb: You implement the algorithms that process signals in real time — audio effects, noise suppression, codecs, filters — often on constrained hardware with hard latency limits. It's a math-heavy specialty where C++ meets frequency-domain thinking and you can literally hear the bugs.

roles.name: IoT Engineer
roles.blurb: You build the systems that connect physical devices to the cloud — edge firmware, connectivity protocols like MQTT and BLE, and the backend that ingests device telemetry at scale. The role spans the full stack from a sensor's power budget to a fleet dashboard, and security is a constant concern.

roles.name: Developer Advocate
roles.blurb: You are the bridge between a product's engineering team and the developers who use it — writing sample apps, giving conference talks, publishing tutorials, and funneling community pain points back into the roadmap. Half your week is building demos and content, the other half is being visibly, helpfully present wherever developers gather.

roles.name: Developer Relations Manager
roles.blurb: You run the DevRel function — setting community strategy, managing a team of advocates, owning developer-marketing metrics, and defending the budget to leadership. Less hands-on demo-building, more program design, hiring, and proving that developer love converts into adoption.

stages.title: Senior DevRel Manager / Head of DevRel

roles.name: Technical Writer
roles.blurb: You turn messy engineering knowledge into clear docs, API references, guides, and release notes that let users succeed without filing a ticket. Modern tech writing is docs-as-code — you work in Markdown and Git, read source, and often ship your changes through the same pipeline as engineers.

roles.name: Sales Engineer
roles.blurb: You are the technical half of the sales team — running demos, scoping solutions, building proofs-of-concept, and answering the hard architecture questions that make or break a deal. Comp is part base, part commission, so you live between the engineering truth and the revenue target.

roles.name: Solutions Engineer
roles.blurb: Closely related to sales engineering but weighted toward architecture: you analyze a customer's requirements, design how the product fits their stack, and build the integration proofs that de-risk adoption. You translate fuzzy business needs into concrete technical solutions on both sides of the sale.

roles.name: Technical Support Engineer
roles.blurb: You are the deep-end of customer support — reproducing bugs, reading logs and stack traces, writing SQL, and escalating to engineering with a tight repro. It's problem-solving under time pressure with a customer watching, and the best support engineers effectively debug the product for a living.

roles.name: Technical Account Manager
roles.blurb: You own the technical health of named enterprise accounts — the trusted advisor who knows their architecture, drives adoption, manages escalations, and keeps them renewing. Part relationship management, part hands-on technical guidance, you sit between the customer and every internal team.

roles.name: Implementation Engineer
roles.blurb: You take a signed customer from zero to live — configuring the product, wiring up integrations and data migrations, and running the technical side of onboarding to first value. It's project delivery with real code and APIs in the mix, and your success metric is time-to-live without surprises.

roles.name: Customer Success Engineer
roles.blurb: You keep customers successful after go-live — driving adoption, solving technical blockers, and spotting expansion and churn signals early. It blends the empathy of customer success with enough engineering depth to actually fix the integration rather than just log the ticket.

roles.name: Scrum Master
roles.blurb: You keep an agile team flowing — running standups, sprint planning, retros, and reviews, removing impediments, and shielding the team from thrash. It's a servant-leadership role: no direct authority, but you own the process health and the team's delivery cadence.

roles.name: Agile Coach
roles.blurb: You coach beyond a single team — helping departments or whole organizations adopt agile ways of working, improve flow, and change culture. It's senior, influence-driven work: training, facilitating, and nudging leadership, often across many teams at once (and frequently on contract rates).

roles.name: Technical Program Manager
roles.blurb: You drive complex, cross-team technical programs to completion — owning the plan, dependencies, risks, and communication for initiatives that span many engineering teams. TPMs need real technical fluency to earn engineers' trust and enough executive presence to keep leadership aligned. It's one of the hottest, best-paid non-coding roles in tech.

roles.name: Program Manager (Technical)
roles.blurb: You coordinate multi-project programs across teams — owning schedules, budgets, risks, and status reporting so leadership always knows where things stand. Less deep-technical than a TPM, more focused on orchestration, communication, and keeping many moving parts synchronized.

roles.name: Data Governance Manager
roles.blurb: You set the rules of the road for data — ownership, quality standards, catalogs, lineage, privacy, and regulatory compliance across the organization. It's part policy, part stakeholder wrangling, and increasingly central as AI and regulation raise the stakes on knowing exactly what data you have and how it can be used.

roles.name: Data Steward
roles.blurb: You are the hands-on owner of data quality for a domain — profiling data, fixing definitions, maintaining the catalog and master data, and enforcing governance policies day to day. Where the governance manager sets policy, you make the data actually trustworthy at the record level.

roles.name: ML Data / Labeling Lead
roles.blurb: You own the data that trains the models — curating datasets, designing annotation strategy and QA, running labeling vendors, and guarding data quality across the ML lifecycle. As model performance becomes a data problem more than a modeling one, this role has gone from afterthought to strategic.

ladder.title: Head of ML Data / Data Operations

roles.name: Data Labeling Operations Manager
roles.blurb: You run the annotation machine — designing labeling workflows and guidelines, managing an internal or vendor workforce, and hitting throughput and quality targets for the datasets ML teams depend on. The RLHF and eval boom turned this into a real operational discipline with metrics, tooling, and headcount.

roles.name: Technical Recruiter
roles.blurb: You find, screen, and close engineering talent — sourcing hard-to-find candidates, running the pipeline in the ATS, coaching hiring managers, and negotiating offers. Enough technical literacy to talk credibly about stacks and levels is what separates a great tech recruiter from a generalist; pay usually blends base with placement bonuses.
